source.title: Larger language models better align with neural representations of natural language
source.authors: Zhuoqiao Hong; Hao-Cheng Wang; Zaid Zada; H. Gazula; David Turner; Bobbi Aubrey; Leonard Niekerken; Werner K. Doyle; S. Devore; Patricia C. Dugan; Daniel Friedman; O. Devinsky; A. Flinker; U. Hasson; Samuel A. Nastase; Ariel Goldstein

record.tranche_reason: The study extends model-scaling analysis to neural prediction: it measures how language-model representations predict ECoG responses across model sizes. It does not test the original pretraining-loss or compute-allocation laws.
record.gate_note: The study reports perplexity on the podcast transcript and neural encoding performance, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Perplexity is recorded as a related result, not as a test of V1. The neural prediction results bear on V6 as a downstream predictive evaluation. Detailed layer and lag analyses are not rows for the listed versions because they measure layer preference or timing rather than downstream performance scaling.
record.test_reason: The study treats brain-encoding accuracy as a downstream evaluation of LLM representations. It measures how that accuracy changes with model size across 82M–70B parameters in four families, plus a size-only sweep within GPT-Neo. This is a new setting for V6. It does not fit or test pretraining-loss laws (V1–V4, V7).
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is mostly right. Larger LLMs better predict ECoG responses, roughly logarithmically in size, consistent across families and within GPT-Neo with fixed training data. Encoding gains plateau around 7B, with a significant decline only for OPT-66B. Perplexity keeps falling with size, and the authors attribute the plateau to their small stimulus. They also report that the best-encoding relative layer moves earlier as size grows, while best lag does not change.
record.recipe_differences: Measures neural encoding performance from model embeddings and perplexity on a podcast transcript, rather than fitting held-out pretraining-loss laws or optimizing parameter/token allocation against training compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary across model family and size, brain region, and encoding approach (ridge regression versus PCA plus OLS); the paper also reports plateauing with increased training data for encoding models in some analyses.

fits_no_version.finding: Perplexity on the podcast transcript decreases with model size across the four families. It keeps decreasing even where brain-encoding performance plateaus.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Perplexity on a naturalistic transcript decreases monotonically with model size, and does so beyond the point where neural encoding gains plateau.

record.problems: The neural analysis uses one approximately 30-minute story of about 5,000 words and 160 selected electrodes from eight patients. Numerical values for several plotted outcomes are not stated in the text. Neural encoding performance plateaus at large sizes, and the OPT-66B result declines.
record.rows_left_out: Layer-preference and lag analyses were not included because they measure best-layer position or timing rather than the downstream-performance scaling named in V6. Supplementary Fig. 4's trained-versus-untrained SMALL comparison and Supplementary Fig. 5's speech-feature comparisons are controls, not model-size scaling outcomes. Supplementary Fig. 6 varies encoding-model training data rather than language-model pretraining tokens.

untested.parts: Standard downstream benchmark tasks; whether encoding performance is predicted from pretraining loss (perplexity and encoding are never directly related); extrapolation from small to large models; any fitted law beyond a described logarithmic trend.
Held-out pretraining loss power laws in parameters, data or compute.
Dependence of exponents on fitting choices.

missing.what: PCA (50 dims) + OLS replication of the size–encoding logarithmic trend, with significantly lower overall performance than ridge for all 20 models. Reviewer notes a larger drop for larger models. Shows dependence on encoding method.
Family-level consistency of the size–encoding trend (stated consistent across GPT-2, GPT-Neo, OPT, Llama 2) with per-family values

record.verdict_notes: Classifying brain encoding as a V6 'downstream task' is a judgment call; a stricter reading could move this study to fits_no_version. The study reports no fitted functional form with parameters, only a described logarithmic relationship. Stimulus size (~5,000 words, 160 GloVe-selected electrodes) limits power at large model sizes.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss, power-law fits, and loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run loss fits or predictions of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute comparison or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No scaling-law tests across modalities or training regimes.
Tests neural encoding of one naturalistic story, not downstream benchmark tasks generally, or whether downstream performance is predictable from pretraining loss.
Does not compare loss-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations across fitting choices.

rows.subject: GPT-2, GPT-Neo, OPT, and Llama 2 models (cross-family sweep)
rows.stage_stated: pretrained versions; Llama 2 versions before reinforcement learning from human feedback
rows.operation_detail: Measured perplexity on the podcast transcript across model sizes.
rows.value: figure only; text states perplexity decreases as model size increases
rows.note: The paper describes this as a decrease in perplexity, but does not report a power-law fit or held-out pretraining loss.
rows.check: This is perplexity on a single ~5,000-word transcript, across families with different training data. No power-law fit is given. It shows only a monotonic decrease, so it does not test V1. Keep it under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: OPT-66B
rows.operation_detail: Compared maximum neural encoding performance with smaller models.

conditions.value: maximum correlation across lags and layers, averaged across electrodes

rows.measure: Pearson correlation between predicted and observed word-level ECoG signals

rows.subject: GPT-Neo family: SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE, and XL
rows.size_stated: 125 million, 1.3 billion, 2.7 billion, and 20 billion parameters, respectively
rows.operation_detail: Compared the larger XL model with SMALL across encoding lags.

conditions.value: most lags from 2000 ms before word onset to 575 ms after word onset

rows.value: Text reports XL significantly outperformed SMALL for most stated lags; exact correlations not stated
rows.uncertainty: paired two-sided t-test across electrodes, df = 159, p < 0.001, Bonferroni corrected
rows.note: This is a neural prediction result, not a held-out language-model loss result.

rows.subject: GPT-Neo MEDIUM, LARGE, and XL, compared with SMALL
rows.size_stated: SMALL 125 million; MEDIUM 1.3 billion; LARGE 2.7 billion; XL 20 billion parameters
rows.operation_detail: Compared encoding performance across electrodes for each larger model against SMALL.

conditions.value: each of MEDIUM, LARGE, and XL versus SMALL

rows.value: Text reports significantly higher performance for larger models in approximately one-third of the 160 electrodes; separate proportions by model not stated
rows.uncertainty: Two-sided pairwise t-test across cross-validation folds for each electrode, p < 0.05, Bonferroni corrected
rows.note: The result is an aggregate statement across the three comparisons; the paper does not give separate counts for each model.
rows.check: Significant gains are reported in about one-third of the 160 electrodes, pooled across three comparisons. The Fig. 3B caption says 'almost all electrodes', which conflicts with the text. Per-model counts are not given.

relationships.condition: Cross-family sweep up to ~7B parameters, and the GPT-Neo SMALL-to-XL sweep with fixed training data
relationships.reason: Encoding correlation rises roughly logarithmically with size (R2). XL beats SMALL at most lags (R5) and in mSTG, aSTG and BA44 (R7–R9).
relationships.display_finding: Encoding correlation increased roughly logarithmically with size, and GPT-Neo XL outperformed SMALL at most lags and in mSTG, aSTG and BA44.

relationships.condition: Models above ~7B parameters; per-electrode and per-region analyses
relationships.reason: Gains plateau around 7B (R3). Only about one-third of electrodes show significant gains (R6). BA45 and TP plateau after MEDIUM, and TP shows no significant XL advantage (R10, R11).
relationships.display_finding: Gains plateaued around 7B, only about one-third of electrodes improved significantly, and BA45 and TP plateaued after MEDIUM, with no significant XL advantage in TP.

relationships.reason: The authors state OPT-66B is significantly worse than some smaller models (R4). This is a single-family reversal.
relationships.display_finding: The largest OPT model performed significantly worse than some smaller models in the same family.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Cross-family size sweep and GPT-Neo XL versus SMALL lag comparison
reader_labels.reason: Neural encoding performance generally increased with model size, and XL significantly outperformed SMALL across most reported lags (R2, R5).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Performance plateaued around 7 billion parameters, and the BA45 and TP regional trends plateaued after MEDIUM; TP showed no significant XL advantage (R3, R10, R11).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: The authors report declining encoding performance for OPT-66B, significantly below some smaller models (R4).
